title: Una and the Moon's Secret
markdown:
Una the little vole lived in a meadow where the clover smelled like honey and fireflies danced like fallen stars. Her home was a warm snug burrow lined with soft moss, a safe cozy place she loved to sleep. Una was a thoughtful creature. Her whiskers twitched when she was thinking about something special. She spent her days rustling through the tall grasses, gathering seeds and listening to the world hum softly around her.

One calm evening, as the sky turned soft shades of pink and purple, Una peeked out. She looked up at the big moon. It shone like a pale pearl, making the twilight a soft pale light. “Oh, lovely moon,” she whispered. A calm feeling wrapped around her like a warm blanket. She watched a while. Soft light made the dewdrops on the clover twinkle like little jewels.

But the very next night, when she looked again, the moon seemed a little less round. A little piece seemed gone from its side. Una’s whiskers gave a little quiver. Her heart gave a tiny thump-thump. “Oh dear,” she whispered. “Is someone taking little bites from the moon?” The thought made her feel a little unsteady, but mostly it made her wonder. She watched over the next few nights, and each time the moon seemed smaller, until it was just a thin sliver of pale light, like a thin smile in the sky. She wondered where all the bright light was going.

She nuzzled a dandelion puff and sighed. Cinder the swift dropped from the sky with a light whistle, dark feathers catching the last warm beams. “What’s making you sad, little Una?” she chirped from a tall stem.

Una told her about moon-biters. Cinder listened, sharp eyes on the sliver. “Bitten? I fly where the clouds drift. I have not seen biters. I do see the moon look different. If we watch together, night after night — my high nest, your warm door — we can learn.”

And so watching the moon together started, a wonderful new time under the darkening sky. Every evening, as the sun dipped low and the world became very quiet, Una would get cozy by her home’s door, round eyes ready. Cinder would perch on a tall grass stem nearby, sharp eyes already on the sky. “Look, Una,” Cinder would call softly, her voice a gentle whisper that joined the quiet. “Tonight the moon is getting bigger again. It looks like a bright pearl, getting rounder. See how the light is getting wider?”

Una watched, and her sad feelings floated away like morning mist, because the sun was fading and her kind steady friend was near. She saw how, after being a thin sliver, the moon slowly, smoothly got rounder. Then, just as slowly, its light began to get thinner again, until it was a thin sliver once more. They saw it as a bright crescent, like a piece of a new apple, then a half-moon shaped like a neat little bowl, then a full bright circle. It was a beautiful silent dance in the sky.

Una started to keep little notes, drawing the moon’s different shapes on flat smooth stones she found near the stream. She saw that it wasn’t being bitten at all, but was following a lovely always-the-same pattern, a beat like her own heart. A gentle dance. A game of light hide-and-seek.

“A game of light hide-and-seek,” she whispered one night, warm with understanding.

Cinder tilted her head. “That is how the sky works. Wonders with a soft beat, round and round.” They learned to wait: after the thinnest sliver, the full moon would come back and fill the meadow. They could even guess the thin nights and the fat ones.

Una and Cinder kept watching. Friendship grew under the stars. The moon was not being eaten. It was completing a trip of light. “It feels like magic,” Una would whisper, snuggling into moss. “Real magic. The kind the world shows if we look.” Cinder’s chirp floated down like a song. Ant trails in the grass, the moon’s slow dance — patterns everywhere. As silver lay on the sleeping meadow, Una felt safe, and Cinder felt glad of the quiet. The stars blinked sleepy goodnights. Both friends drifted toward dreams, ready for the next night, and whatever shape the sky would borrow then.
